bio.en: Jeffrey Pfeffer is a Professor of Organizational Behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business and the author of The 7 Rules of Power, who teaches that power is a learnable skill—not a personality trait—that advances your career and well-being.
bio.zh: Jeffrey Pfeffer 是斯坦福商学院组织行为学教授、《权力的 7 条法则》（The 7 Rules of Power）的作者，他主张权力是一项可习得的技能——而非性格特质——能推动你的职业生涯与幸福感。

summary.en: Jeffrey lays out his seven rules of power—get out of your own way, break the rules, show up powerfully, build a brand, network relentlessly, use your power, and accept that how you got it will be forgiven—and insists these are masterable skills, not personality. He argues that if you think power is 'dirty' you'll unconsciously sabotage your own success, and that more good people need power so it's used for good. The conversation walks through each rule with real examples and ends with concrete steps you can start today to build your own power, whether you're an IC or a CEO.
summary.zh: Jeffrey 列出了他的七条权力法则——别挡自己的路、打破规则、以强者的姿态出现、建立个人品牌、不懈地经营人脉、运用你的权力、并接受一个事实：你获取权力的方式终会被原谅——并强调这些都是可掌握的技能，而非性格。他主张，如果你认为权力“肮脏”，就会在潜意识里 sabotage 自己的成功；而需要更多好人掌握权力，权力才能被用于善。对话逐条讲解每条法则并配以真实案例，最后给出你今天就能开始的、建立自身权力的具体步骤——无论你是个人贡献者还是 CEO。

turns.zh:
这门课程非常受欢迎。我有很长的等候名单。它近乎传奇般的存在。基于社会影响原理，我们会受到他人行为的影响——无论是餐厅选择、音乐品味，我都不确定自己是否喜欢泰勒·斯威夫特，但大家都去看她的演唱会，我也想去。所以很多人报名这门课。有一年，有几个人坐在我前排第三排，每天表情痛苦，仿佛在忍受某种可怕的折磨。他们显然非常不适。于是我决定，尽管他们什么也没学到，但我还是要告诉大家：要想从这门课中受益，就必须保持开放的学习态度。如果你抱着消极态度，任何课程都不会有收获。比如学物理时你说："我不喜欢物理，讨厌物理，不相信物理学理论"，那你注定学不到东西。因此面对长长的等候名单，我努力确保学员真正能从课程中获益，而不是坐在那里一脸痛苦。  

谈到评判他人时，《马太福音》7章说："不要论断人，免得你们被论断。"《古兰经》说："只有真主才能审判人。"美国诗人沃尔特·惠特曼说："保持好奇心，而非妄加评判。"特蕾莎修女说："若评判他人，你便无暇关爱他们。" 

回到职场关系，若某人是我的关键合作伙伴，而工作本身就需要一定程度的相互依存，我需要通过他人完成任务。如果我认为某人愚蠢、无能、道德败坏等，这些负面标签只会毁掉合作关系。除非你演技高超或我比大多数人更擅长隐藏情绪，否则这种关系注定破裂。

因此，面对关键合作伙伴，暂停评判至关重要。只要他们在你的关键路径上，你只需专注合作。个人偏好无关紧要。多年来我教导高管们，关键技能之一就是让人看不透你的真实想法。这至关重要，因为我需要他们的配合，若流露出不尊重或厌恶情绪，合作几率将归零。

This is your fourth book about power, and this is your best book about power, because it basically summarizes everything you've learned in a really cohesive way. So let me first share the Seven Rules of Power and then I'm going to dive into a few of them. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 这正好引出您的一条权力法则。让我们来聊聊您的七条权力法则。我这里正好有您的书，如果大家想深入了解，可以看看《七条权力法则》。这是您关于权力的第四本书，也是最出色的一本，它以高度凝练的方式总结了您多年研究成果。接下来，我先分享七条法则，再深入解析其中几条。您意下如何？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: That sounds perfect.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so the seven rules, one, get out of your own way. Two, break the rules. Three, appear powerful. Four, build a powerful brand. Network relentlessly. Use your power, and success excuses almost...
turns.zh: 好的，那就从第一条开始：别给自己找借口。第二条：打破规则。第三条：展现权势。第四条：打造强大品牌。第五条：不懈拓展人脉。第六条：运用权力，成功几乎可以掩盖一切……

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Everything, correct.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, success excuses everything almost. Got it. Okay. So let me start with power four, which is around personal brand. And the reason I want to start here is I have a friend that's actually in your class right now, Ralph, and I saw that he started a podcast. And he told me that he did it because it was part of the homework that you give students. You call it Doing Power. Is that the name of the homework assignments?
turns.zh: 好的，成功几乎能掩盖一切。明白了。那就从第四条开始，讲讲个人品牌。之所以从这里入手，是因为我有个朋友Ralph现在也在上您的课，我发现他开了个播客。他告诉我，这是作业的一部分，叫“实践权力”。是这个作业名称吗？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah, I have. So we give them a bunch of assignments throughout the class, which are self-reflective assignments, but their big thing for the class is they have to do power. They have to do something during the quarter to take the principles of the class, and what they're learning, and put them into practice. And that is because everything I do, I do for a reason. That is because if you don't use what you learn, the learning will disappear. So if you go to a French class and you learn French, and you never speak French, in about a relatively short period of time you'll forget everything you learn. And so I want the learning to stick with them, so I try to get them to do something with it.
turns.zh: 是的。我们在课上布置了大量作业，多数是自我反思类任务，但最核心的是“实践权力”。学生们必须在学期内完成某项任务，将课程原理与实际生活相结合。这是因为我做任何事都有其深层逻辑。如果不将所学付诸实践，知识很快就会遗忘。比如学法语却从不说法语，知识很快就会消失。因此，我希望知识能真正落地生根，所以会让学生通过实践来巩固所学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While we're on this tangent, I wanted to talk about this whole, you have a book, the Doing Knowing Gap.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我想聊聊您的《知行差距》一书。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Knowing-Doing Gap.
turns.zh: 知行差距。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Knowing-Doing Gap. So let's just spend a little time there. I think that's really important. What are some examples of things that have come out of people doing these homework assignments, things that maybe led to something interesting?
turns.zh: 知行差距。接下来我们就花点时间探讨一下这个话题。我觉得这非常重要。通过完成这些作业，有哪些例子能带来有趣的成果呢？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Let me take my most extreme example. My most extreme example is probably Derek Kan, K-A-N. And Derek Kan was a little bit older when he went through the MBA program. And in 2012, his Doing Power project was to get appointed to be Mitt Romney's, it was Mitt Romney was running for president, to be head of economic policy for the Romney campaign. Believe it or not, he was offered the job. Believe it or not, he turned it down for reasons which we could go into if you want, but aren't that interesting. He wound up relatively soon thereafter as number three in the transportation department, working for Elaine Chao. And I have a picture of him when he comes to the class, I introduce him. I tell students, I give them a trigger warning and I introduce him. He wound up, at the end of the Trump administration, as the deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget. And since typical of the Trump administration, by that time there was no director. He essentially ran the $6 trillion US budget. This is six years out of business school.
turns.zh: 让我举个最极端的例子。最极端的例子可能要数德里克·坎（Derek Kan）了。他参加MBA项目时年龄稍大一些。2012年，他在“Doing Power”项目中成功获得了米特·罗姆尼竞选团队经济政策主管的职位。要知道，当时米特·罗姆尼正在竞选总统。信不信由你，他得到了这个职位。但出于某些原因（如果你想了解具体原因的话，也挺有趣的，但今天先不说），他最终拒绝了这个邀请。不久之后，他就成了交通部第三号人物，为伊莱恩·庄（Elaine Chao）工作。有他来上课的照片，我会介绍他。我会提醒学生注意可能引发的不适情绪，然后正式介绍他。在特朗普政府执政末期，他又被任命为管理和预算办公室副主任。特朗普政府的特点就是，到了那个时候，主任职位已经空缺了。他实际上负责着美国6万亿美元的预算。这距离他毕业才六年啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was thinking whether he got that during his class. Amazing. Okay, so this is a success story of Doing Power. Let's talk about this first power of building brand, and I think this is where people start to feel uncomfortable. They're going to be like, oh no, I don't want to be doing this. This doesn't feel good to me.
turns.zh: 我在想他是在上课期间获得这个机会的吗？太不可思议了。好吧，这就是“Doing Power”的成功案例。接下来我们来谈谈建立个人品牌的首要力量，我觉得这正是人们开始感到不自在的地方。他们会想，天哪，我不想做这件事。这让我感觉很不舒服。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's talk about it.
turns.zh: 那我们就来聊聊这个话题。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's see. So talk about this power of building a personal brand.
turns.zh: 让我看看。那么，谈谈建立个人品牌的力量吧。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: There are by definition fewer positions at the top than at the bottom. The world, we might not like this, and I know people, the late Tony Hsieh, the Zappos tried to do holacracy or whatever, but the world is essentially hierarchical. The animal kingdom is hierarchical. It is better to be at the top than at the bottom for a number of reasons. Okay. If that is true, if there are fewer positions at the top and then at the bottom, then your job to advance your career is to figure out how to get promoted. There are many ways to get promoted, but I will guarantee you one thing, no one is going to promote Lenny if they don't know who the hell you are. So it is not sufficient for them to know who you are. They have to know that you're smart and personable and have whatever skills you've got, but they have to know you. (00:16:52): If they don't know you, you cannot choose what is not in your head. You know that better than I do. So therefore you have to do something to differentiate yourself. You have to build a brand. So when I think of Lenny in your podcast, I think of something. Not just 25 billion podcasts. When I think of somebody in McKinsey or Bay or BCG, one of the consulting firms, a gazillion people start off as front-line consultants. What are you going to do so that somebody knows who you are? What are you going to do that creates value for the firm and for you? So my friend Keith Ferazzi, when he started at Deloitte Consulting, did not do the spreadsheet stuff that he was, by the way, not very good at and didn't like. He started the Lincoln Quality Award. He decided to try to take Deloitte's brand recognition from about one or 2% to 30%. (00:17:54): He was appointed, though he left before he actually took the job, to the position of partner and the first chief marketing officer at Deloitte. I have another friend, Tristan Walker, who wanted to get hired at Foursquare. He sent emails to the founder. The founder ignored him. So Tristan Walker did something I think very bold. Tristan Walker began signing up partnerships. So one day the founder says, holy God, he signed up Starbucks. Maybe I ought to hire this guy. So you have to do something that causes people to know who you are, and that is what building a brand is about.
turns.zh:
按照定义，顶层职位总是比底层职位少。我们可能不喜欢这种现实，但现实就是如此——就像已故的谢长廷（Tony Hsieh）和Zappos尝试推行霍拉克拉（holacracy）之类的管理模式，但世界本质上就是等级分明的。动物王国也是等级分明的。出于多种原因，身处顶层总比底层要好。如果这一观点成立，那么要想在职业生涯中晋升，就必须想办法获得晋升机会。晋升的途径有很多，但我可以肯定一点：如果别人根本不了解你，他们绝不会提拔你莱尼（Lenny）。所以光让别人知道你是谁是不够的。他们不仅要知道你能干，还要了解你的个性和技能，但首先他们得认识你。

（00:16:52）：如果别人不认识你，你就无法选择那些你尚未想到的东西。你比我更清楚这一点。因此，你必须想办法脱颖而出。你必须打造个人品牌。比如在你的播客中提到莱尼时，我脑海中浮现出什么画面？不只是25亿个播客。当我想到麦肯锡、贝恩或波士顿咨询等咨询公司的人时，无数人都是从一线顾问做起的。你要如何让别人记住你是谁？你要如何为公司和自己创造价值？我的朋友基思·费拉齐（Keith Ferazzi）刚加入德勤咨询时，没有做他不擅长也不喜欢的电子表格工作，而是发起了林肯质量奖。他决心将德勤的品牌知名度从1%左右提升至30%。

（00:17:54）：他被任命为德勤合伙人兼首位首席营销官，但最终未能上任。我还有个朋友特里斯坦·沃克（Tristan Walker）想加入Foursquare。他给创始人发邮件，创始人却无视他。于是特里斯坦做了件大胆之举——开始签约合作伙伴。有一天创始人惊呼：天哪，他签约了星巴克！这才意识到该给这人一个机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds very benign put that way. When people hear, I need to build a personal brand, it sounds like I need to post on LinkedIn, I need to post on Twitter, start a newsletter, start a podcast, which I know is kind of a part of it. But what are some examples you've seen of ways to build a personal brand that are effective?
turns.zh: 这么说听起来很平常。但当人们听到“我需要打造个人品牌”时，总觉得就是在领英发帖、推特互动、发新闻简报、开播客之类的。我知道这些确实是部分内容，但你见过哪些有效的个人品牌打造案例？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: So I have a friend who I bring to the class, a lovely tall Asian woman named Laura Chau, who made partner at a venture capital firm after four years, which is fast. Laura works for Canaan Partners, C-A-N-A-A-N. Laura said, I do not work for Andreessen Horowitz, I do not work for Sequoia, I don't work for Greylock, I don't work for any of these very visible large VC firms. So if I am going to get deals in the consumer space, that's her domain of expertise is consumer and consumer tech, somebody is going to have to know who Laura Chau is. Because again, you're not going to get the deal if nobody knows who you are. And so she basically did everything you talked about. She did writing. She started a podcast in which she invited influential people on. She contributed to a book. She helped people out. (00:19:55): She did networking dinners. She did everything she could so that people would recognize and know Laura Chau. And one of the things she did was she's tall. In general, Asian women are not tall. She decided to play up the fact that she was, in the words of some people, the tallest Asian woman they'd ever seen. She wears heels. In her heels she's six feet one inches tall. She also, when she comes to my class, many people come to my class with hoodies, God knows what. She has style and it's a unique style. So she thinks about very strategically, how am I going to dress? How am I going to look? How am I going to show up? How am I going to do what I need to do so that people know who I am? Obviously there's substance. If you have visibility without substance, people will know you're useless. But if you have substance without visibility, no one will know the substance that you got.
turns.zh: 我有个朋友，我会带她来上课，她叫劳拉·周，是一位可爱的亚裔高个子女性。她在一家风险投资公司担任合伙人，仅用四年时间就达到了这个职位，这速度相当快。劳拉就职于Canaan Partners，公司名是C-A-N-A-A-N。她说，我不为安德森·霍洛维茨工作，不为红杉资本工作，也不为Greylock Partners或其他那些备受瞩目的风险投资公司工作。所以，如果我想在消费领域拿下交易，那就得靠她了。因为再强调一遍，如果没人认识你，就拿不下交易。所以她基本上做了你提到的所有事情。她写作。她创办了一个播客，邀请有影响力的人参与。她为一本书撰稿。她帮助他人。（00:19:55）她参加社交晚宴。她竭尽全力让人们认识并记住劳拉·周。她做的其中一件事是，她个子很高。一般来说，亚洲女性个子不高。但她决定突出这一点——用某些人的话说，她是他们见过的最高的亚洲女性。她穿高跟鞋。穿上高跟鞋，她身高就达到了6英尺1英寸。还有，她来上我的课时，很多人来上课时穿着连帽衫，天知道他们穿的什么。她很有风格，而且风格独特。所以她会非常策略地思考：我该怎么穿？我该怎么打扮？我该怎么展现自己？我该怎么做才能让人们记住我？显然，光有实质内容没有可见度是没用的。但只有可见度没有实质内容，也没人会知道你的实力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also talk about how you can reframe this idea of not being self-promotional, but it's amplifying the impact of the team that I work with, or it's me scaling myself by sharing things I know and pointing people to it.
turns.zh: 你还提到如何重新定义不自我推销的概念，而是要放大我所在团队的影响力，或者通过分享自己所知并引导他人来提升自己。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Absolutely, absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, let's move on to a different power. Let's talk about power one, which is getting out of your own way. Talk about what that means and how someone can work on that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们来谈谈另一种权力——克服自我障碍。请解释一下这意味着什么，以及人们该如何努力做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, you already have done a fabulous job of illustrating principle one by talking about how this is the topic that makes people uncomfortable. And when something makes people uncomfortable, in general, they're going to shy away from it. So if I think power is dirty, if I think power is evil, if I think power is something I want nothing to do with, the first thing that's going to happen is I'm not going to do what I need to do to be successful in my career. So that is one way in which we get in our own way. Another way in which we get in our own way, many people suffer from what is called in the psychology literature, imposter syndrome. They believe that they were the admissions mistake at Stanford. They were the hiring mistake in whatever company they're working for. That somehow they got to this job, but they don't really deserve to be there because they're surrounded by people who are smarter and better than them, and therefore they will do things. (00:22:18): I can't even believe that this goes on. So I will have students, not many, but a few. Now raise their hand, I'll call them, and the first things out of their mouth will be, I don't know if this comment is going to be useful. This is called pre-emptory apology. If the comment is not going to be useful, don't say it. That's number one, but number two, don't apologize. Pardon me for interrupting. Pardon me for taking up your time. Stop all this apologizing. If you got the job you're in, you probably are not only qualified, you're probably overqualified. So don't use descriptors of yourself that disempower you. Don't think of yourself as not deserving of the job that you hold, because that attitude will leak out and other people will say, if Lenny doesn't think he deserved the job, then maybe I shouldn't think he deserves the job either.
turns.zh: 好的，你已经出色地阐释了第一条原则——你谈到这个话题会让人感到不适，而当某件事让人不适时，人们通常会回避它。所以，如果我认为权力是肮脏的、邪恶的，或者是自己不想沾染的东西，首先我就会不去采取成功所需的行动。这就是我们自我设限的一种方式。另一种自我设限的方式是，很多人深受心理学文献中所谓的“冒名顶替综合症”困扰。他们觉得自己是斯坦福大学的录取失误，是所在公司的招聘失误，觉得自己能获得这份工作只是运气好，但实际上不配在这里，因为周围的人比自己更聪明、更优秀。因此，他们会采取行动。（00:22:18）：我简直不敢相信这种情况还存在。我遇到过一些学生，虽然不多，但也有几个。现在让他们举手，我会点名，第一句话往往是：“我不知道这条评论是否有用。”这就是先发制人的道歉。如果评论没用，就别说。第一点是别道歉。打断别人说：“对不起，打扰你了。”别再道歉了。如果你能胜任现有工作，那你很可能不仅够格，甚至是能力过剩。所以别用贬低自己的词汇。别觉得自己配不上现有职位，因为这种态度会传递出来，别人会想：“如果莱尼都觉得自己不配，那或许我也该这么想。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So basically the first power is you're shooting yourself in the foot by worrying too much about whether people like you. This friend of mine who's now the founder that I read some quotes from, she said her number one takeaway from your class is if you want to be liked, get a dog.
turns.zh: 所以第一条权力法则是：过度担心别人是否喜欢你，就是自己搬石头砸自己的脚。我提到的那位现在是创始人的朋友，她读过你的一些引语，说她从你的课上最大的收获是，如果想被喜欢，就养条狗。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: That's correct. That is a quote from my dear friend Gary Loveman, who for many years ran Harrah's, which then became Caesars, the casino company.
turns.zh: 没错。这句话出自我的好友加里·洛夫曼，他曾多年执掌哈拉斯赌场，后来该公司改名为凯撒娱乐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also talk about this. Yeah, there's this quote I have. "Acknowledge that others are often no better than you, because that makes you feel better about the story." So for people that actually want to be liked, I like being liked. I don't know if it's a flaw in my upbringing. Is the lesson you're capped on your power if you worry about if you want to be liked?
turns.zh: 你也提到过这个。是啊，我有句话：“承认别人通常也不比你强，因为这样能让你对自己的处境感觉好一些。” 所以对于那些想被喜欢的人，我喜欢被喜欢。我不知道这是不是成长环境的缺陷。你的课程传递的核心观点是，如果担心自己是否被喜欢，那就是在削弱自己的权力吗？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: At the end of the day, you don't want to be intentionally disliked. You don't want to violate my dear friend Bob Sutton's book The No Asshole Rule and gratuitously be an asshole. But you are hired to get a job done. It's interesting. I unfortunately am now too old. In the words of my chiropractor, I'm suffering from too many birthdays. So I have a lot of doctors who are doing a great job. Trust me, when I choose a doctor, I have a, unfortunately he retired, a neurosurgeon who did two surgeries on my spine. He's considered to be one of the top 20 in the country. If you go on Yelp, you read about his personality and his office furniture. As I said to somebody, he's doing microsurgery on my spine, I can wind up permanently paralyzed. I really don't care about his personality. I don't care about his office furniture. (00:25:01): That's an extreme example, but it makes the point. When you are put in a role, you are put in a role because presumably you are supposed to perform in that role. If you get appointed to be a head coach, if we make you a quarterback on an NFL team, or we make you center on a National Basketball Association team, you did not get that job because people thought you had a cute personality. You got that job because you have the skills to make your organization successful. And if you do not use those skills because you're worried about what everybody else is thinking, you are not only harming yourself, but you're harming them because you are not doing what you were hired to do.
turns.zh: 归根结底，你不想故意招人讨厌。你不想违反我亲爱的朋友鲍勃·萨顿（Bob Sutton）在《不做混蛋规则》（The No Asshole Rule）一书中的原则，毫无必要地成为一个混蛋。但你受雇于此，是为了完成工作。这很有趣。可惜我现在年纪太大了。用脊椎按摩师的话说，我"生日过多"了。所以我有很多医生，他们工作做得很出色。相信我，当我选择医生时，有一位不幸已经退休的神经外科医生，为我的脊椎做了两次手术。他被认为是全美前20名中的一个。如果你去Yelp上看看，会读到关于他的个性和办公室家具的评价。正如我对某人说的，他要在我的脊椎上做显微手术，如果出了问题，我可能会永久瘫痪。我真的不在乎他的个性。也不在乎他的办公室家具。（00:25:01）：这是一个极端的例子，但它说明了问题。当你被赋予一个角色时，你被赋予这个角色是因为人们认为你应该胜任这个角色。如果你被任命为主教练，如果我们让你成为NFL球队的四分卫，或者让你成为NBA球队的中锋，你得到这份工作不是因为人们认为你性格可爱，而是因为你有让组织成功的技能。如果你因为担心别人怎么想而不用这些技能，你不仅伤害自己，还会伤害他人——因为你没有履行被雇佣的职责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a simple way of thinking about this, which makes me feel better about. As we talk through this, I'm becoming less uncomfortable with these, which is a good sign. It's don't actively try to be disliked. Don't prioritize being liked, prioritize competence and respect.
turns.zh: 所以一个简单的思考方式，这让我感觉好多了。在我们讨论这个问题时，我越来越不觉得不舒服了，这是个好迹象。就是不要主动招人讨厌。不要把被喜欢放在首位，而是要重视能力和尊重。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Correct, absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And doing the thing that needs to be done.
turns.zh: 去做需要做的事。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Let's talk about rule number two, which is break the rules. So basically again, these powers are ways to grow power, and you're saying that if you break the rules, you get more power. Talk about why that's the case, what that looks like.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。让我们来谈谈第二条规则，即打破规则。所以基本上来说，这些权力是增长权力的方式，而你说如果你打破规则，就会获得更多的权力。谈谈为什么会这样，以及这具体表现为何。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, for many reasons, number one, when you break the rules, you stand out. You become memorable when you do something that's unexpected. And being memorable is of course important, as we've already discussed. That's number one. Number two, the rules were made mostly by the people who are favored by the rules in place. So if we were talking about business strategy, we would talk about a word that is probably now overused. We would talk about being a disruptor. That you would disrupt an industry. And how do you disrupt an industry? By doing something that is different from the other industry incumbents. In Southwest Airlines, you don't do hub and spoke. At Amazon, you provide an incredible level of customer service. Whole Foods, you don't optimize on the cost of the stuff in your store, but you optimize on fitting local taste, whatever. You would be a disruptor, you would do things that are different. (00:27:14): The same principle holds for you, that if you are going to be successful, you have to do what number one, plays to your strengths, to use the title of a Gallup book. Number two, you have to do things again that cause you to stand out, and you have to do things that basically will make you more successful. One of the conventional wisdoms that people I think adhere to way too much, is don't ask. Don't ask, don't ask for help. You need to show self-sufficiency. So my colleague, Frances Flynn, Frank Flynn, wrote an article with Vanessa Lake entitled, If You Need Help, Just Ask. And it turns out people overestimate how many people they're going to have to ask to get help, and it turns out that asking for help makes people uncomfortable. (00:28:03): I was married, if you read the acknowledgments in Seven Rules of Power. For more than 35 years I was married to Kathleen Francis Fowler, who I could send you a picture. She looked literally like a supermodel and I never have been any particularly better looking than I am now. So somebody said to me, how'd you get her to go out with you? And the answer of course is, I asked. I asked, I asked, I asked. No one, well, maybe not no one. But few people are going to go out with you if you don't ask them out. Few people are going to marry you if you don't ask them to marry. Few people are going to do anything if you don't ask. And what is the worst that could happen? If you ask and they say, no, you are no worse off than had you not asked in the first place. If you don't ask, you're not going to get it. If you ask and they say, no, you're not going to get it. Get over your ego, ask.
turns.zh:
嗯，出于多种原因，首先，当你打破规则时，你会脱颖而出。当你做些出乎意料的事时，人们会记住你。我们之前已经讨论过，“被记住”很重要，这就是第一点。其次，规则大多是由既得利益者制定的。比如在商业战略领域，我们常用一个如今被滥用的词——“颠覆者”。你要颠覆一个行业，那就得做些与现有行业巨头截然不同的事。西南航空不采用“枢纽辐射”模式；亚马逊提供极致的客户服务；全食超市不以削减成本为优先，而是迎合本地口味。这些都是颠覆者，他们的行为与行业惯例背道而驰。

同样的道理，若想成功，你也必须做到两点：首先，发挥自身优势，正如盖洛普公司《发挥你的优势》一书所言；其次，采取能让你脱颖而出的行动，最终助你更胜一筹。人们常犯的一个错误，就是过度强调自立。我的同事弗兰克·弗林和凡妮莎·莱克曾写过一篇文章，题为《需要帮助时，就开口求助》。研究发现，人高估了寻求帮助的次数，而主动求助反而让人感到不适。

谈谈我自己：如果你读过《权力七则》的致谢部分，就会知道我与凯瑟琳·弗朗西斯·福勒的婚姻长达35年。我可以给你们看照片，她简直像超模，而我现在也算不上帅哥。有人问我：你怎么追到她的？答案当然是不断尝试。若你不主动，她绝不会答应；若你不主动，她绝不会嫁给你；若你不主动，任何事都无法达成。最坏的结果是什么？即使被拒绝，也比从未尝试过要好。即便被拒绝，你也不会失去任何机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there another example that comes to mind of someone breaking the rules say in business, that ended up being really successful as a result, or just someone that is really good at this in business?
turns.zh: 你能想到其他在商业中打破规则却最终大获成功的例子吗？或者说，在商业中擅长打破规则的人？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: I can give you many examples. One of my favorite examples would be Jason Calacanis. I don't know if you know Jason.
turns.zh: 我能举很多例子。我最喜欢的例子之一是杰森·卡拉卡尼斯。你认识他吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, I know you did a case study on him. I know him well. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对，我知道你写过关于他的案例研究。我和他很熟。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: So I think Jason, I think consistently breaks all kinds of rules. First of all, when he comes to my class, nobody likes him, but that's okay. Almost nobody likes him. But...
turns.zh: 我觉得杰森一直在打破各种规则。首先，他来上我的课时，几乎没人喜欢他，但没关系。几乎没人喜欢他。但……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's power number one. He's not worried about.
turns.zh: 这就是第一条权力法则。他不在乎这些。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah, that's number one. But also I think there's a conventional wisdom in the venture capital industry which he defies almost completely. He makes a lot of little bets, not a few big bets. He runs a very lean operation. He doesn't have a lot of partners. He doesn't have actually any partners, so he can't be fired by his partners. He began his career in journalism, which is interesting. Being a journalist is a wonderful job because you get to ask people all kinds of questions. And if you ask smart people questions, and you have some reasonable level of intelligence yourself, at the end of that process, you're going to wind up incredibly smart and incredibly insightful. And he wound up incredibly smart and insightful around aspects of the internet industry.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是第一点。但我认为，在风险投资行业存在一种传统观念，而他几乎完全违背了这种观念。他进行大量的小额投资，而非少数大额投资。他运营着一个非常精简的团队。他没有很多合伙人。实际上他根本没有合伙人，所以合伙人也无法解雇他。他最初的职业是新闻记者，这很有趣。做记者是一份很棒的工作，因为你可以向人们提出各种各样的问题。如果你向聪明的人提问，而你自己也有一定的智力水平，那么最终你会变得极其聪明和富有洞察力。他在互联网行业方面的见解也极其深刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And he definitely has a lot of power. I think I am going to link to the case study in our show notes where you basically walk through how he went from nothing to a very powerful person.
turns.zh: 而且他确实拥有很大的影响力。我想我会在节目笔记中附上案例研究，详细讲述他如何从一无所有到成为极具影响力人物的过程。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: And by the way, a very rich person as well.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，他也是个非常富有的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about another power, power five, networking relentlessly. What does that look like and how do you get better at this?
turns.zh: 让我们来谈谈另一种影响力——第五种影响力：不懈地建立人脉。这看起来是什么样的？如何在这方面做得更好？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, I think there's research that shows that many people find networking dirty, and that's because I think they think about it in the wrong way. My friend John Levy, who has written a fabulous book, You're Invited. Which is a book about how to put on events that people want to come to. Is a fabulous human being. Will tell you that the first principle of networking is in fact generosity. It's generosity. What can I do for you? How can I be helpful? Who can I introduce you to? Either a company or a product or a person who can be helpful to you in your career. (00:31:20): But in order to be able to introduce you to someone who's going to be useful to you, I have to know people. If I don't know anybody, I can't introduce you to anybody. And the more people I know, the more likely it will be that if you say, I need to know somebody in X, I will know that person. So the broader your social network, the more people and the more things you will know. If knowledge is power, networking is a fabulous way to get knowledge about people and about ideas.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为有研究表明，许多人认为建立人脉很功利，这是因为他们用错误的方式看待它。我的朋友约翰·利维写了一本很棒的书《你被邀请了》，这本书讲的是如何举办人们愿意参加的活动。他是个很棒的人。他会告诉你，建立人脉的第一原则实际上是慷慨。是慷慨。能为你做什么？如何能帮到你？能为你介绍谁？无论是一家公司、一个产品，还是一个能在你的职业生涯中帮到你的人（00:31:20）。但要能为你介绍一个对你有用的人，我必须认识这些人。如果我不认识任何人，我就无法为你介绍任何人。认识的人越多，如果你说，我需要认识X领域的人，我就越有可能认识那个人。所以你的社交网络越广，你认识的人和事物就越多。如果知识是力量，那么建立人脉就是获取关于人和想法的知识的绝佳方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's funny to hear this where it's like, yes, obviously this is right, but connecting it to if you want to become more powerful, more successful, you need to do this. I think that is a powerful point that we're all making here, is just like this actually is necessary if you want to acquire more power.
turns.zh: 听到这里很有趣，好像是说，是的，显然这是对的，但把它与如果你想变得更强大、更成功，你需要这样做联系起来。我认为这是我们在这里要强调的一个重要观点，那就是如果你想获得更多权力，这确实是必要的。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Of course. I have a funny story about networking. So we have a thing in Stanford called View From The Top, in which these fancy people come in and give a talk. And one of the people came in and give a talk and made my class instantly popular, because he's an extraordinarily wealthy person. His name is Omid Kordestani, and so I reached out to him and I said, "Omid, let's have breakfast." So I can understand because during the thing, when somebody asked them what class was the most important in his success, he said mine. So I said, "Tell me your story." He said, "Well, I graduated from Stanford. I'm Persian in background, immigrant background. An engineer, HP, all the things that would make you kind of a nerd or something." He said, "I went to work for a couple of startups that didn't do well. Then I found myself in the mid-nineties at Netscape." The browser company, big deal. Anyway, Marc Andreessen.
turns.zh: 没错。我有个关于社交networking的趣事。在斯坦福大学有个叫"View From The Top"的活动，每次都会有大牛来做演讲。有一次来了一个人，让我的课瞬间爆火，因为他是个超级富豪，叫奥米德·科德斯塔尼（Omid Kordestani）。于是我主动联系他，说：“奥米德，咱们一起吃个早餐吧。”我能理解他为什么这么说——在活动上有人问他，哪门课对他的成功最重要，他回答是我的课。于是我说：“讲讲你的故事吧。”他说：“嗯，我毕业于斯坦福大学，出身伊朗移民家庭，学的是工程学，曾在惠普工作，这些背景会让人觉得我是个书呆子之类的。后来我去了几家创业公司，但都不成功。90年代中期，我加入了网景公司（Netscape）——那个浏览器巨头，就是马克·安德森（Marc Andreessen）创办的公司。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对了。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Okay. "So I found myself in Netscape in marketing and business development. I was not making any progress. One day I decided to take your class to an extreme. I decided to stop doing my job." So I said, "When people gave you projects to do or assignments or tasks and you didn't do them?" He said, "It turns out that I spent my time, not obviously at the bar, but in networking first with people inside of Netscape. And it turns out if you're well-connected to the senior leaders, they don't really care if you do your job or not. That's number one. Number two," he said, "oftentimes I can find other people to do the work I was doing. So instead of basically spending time doing my job, I networked first within Netscape." But Netscape was not that big of a company. So after a while he decided to go through, which is by the way, his job anyway, in marketing and business, he decided to basically drive through the Silicon Valley talking to people. And this is the rest of the browsers are just beginning. (00:34:14): Nobody knows what a browser is, nobody knows what the internet is going to become. So he's having all these fabulous conversations. All right, so he now knows basically everybody. It's 1998 and a little tiny company decides 10 engineers, typical Silicon Valley company. 10 engineers, all engineers. I have a friend who went to work for a company, run a company that had 26 people. He didn't have one sales and marketing person. Anyway, the company now has 10 engineers. They decide they need to hire their first business person. Being an analytically oriented company, they say, we're going to do this very analytically. We are basically going to ask everybody we can think of, and a few people we can't. Give us a list of the best technically oriented business people that you know. And there is of course one name that appears on every list. It is Omid Kordestani who becomes employee number 11 at Google and makes two and a half billion dollars.
turns.zh: 好的。“后来我在网景公司负责市场和业务开发，但毫无进展。有一天我决定彻底豁出去，决定彻底不做本职工作了。”我问：“当别人给你布置项目、任务或作业，而你不去做时？”他说：“结果发现，我把时间花在网景内部社交上。只要你和高层关系好，他们根本不在乎你工作与否。这是关键点。其次……”他说，“我常能找到别人替我做事。所以我没去忙本职工作，而是先在网景内部社交。”但网景毕竟不算大公司。过段时间，他决定跳槽——毕竟这是他的本职工作——在硅谷四处拜访，进行社交。这时其他浏览器才刚起步。（00:34:14）：没人知道什么是浏览器，也不知道互联网会发展成什么样子。于是他进行了各种精彩的对话。到1998年，一个小公司（典型的硅谷公司）决定招10名工程师，全是工程师。我有个朋友去了一家26人的公司——连一个销售或市场人员都没有。现在这家公司又要招首位商务人员。作为一家注重分析的公司，他们决定用科学方法：让所有可能认识的人推荐技术型商务人才。结果一个名字反复出现——奥米德·科德斯塔尼（Omid Kordestani），他后来成为谷歌的第11号员工，身家25亿美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great success from networking. Well done. When people hear about networking, it just feels like you said, very cringe. I don't want to go to these networking events and try to pretend to talk and care about people. Do you have any advice for just how to make networking feel less cringy?
turns.zh: 社交networking带来的巨大成功。干得好！一提到networking，人们总觉得很尴尬。我不想去参加那些社交活动，假装关心别人。你有什么建议让networking不那么尴尬吗？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: One of the exercises I give my students is I say, write a list of 10 people who, if you knew them and if they knew you, would be important for whatever you're trying to accomplish in your career. So maybe you're trying to get into biotech, you need to know 10 executives in biotech or whatever. Make a list of 10 people. Then for each person figure out how you are going to meet them. By the way, not necessarily in a network event. Maybe you want to do what John Levy does, which is hold dinners. In which by the way, the guests do the cooking, which is a very interesting idea. That of course taps into the IKEA effect. You always like something better if you participate in creating it. Maybe you want to hold dinners, maybe you want to try to reach out to them at lunch. (00:36:21): Maybe you want to reach out to them and say, here's an article I think you'd be interested in. Here is somebody who I think you'd benefit from meeting. So recently, I'm not a particularly good networker, though I'm better I guess than some people. I recently met Esther Wojcicki, I'm sure I killed her name. She's considered the grandmother of Silicon Valley. She's Susan Wojcicki's mother. And she is interested in depression, particularly depression among teenagers. And I said, you should know Leanne Williams, who's in the Psychiatry and Behavioral Science Department, who has done probably 300 articles on depression and has invented something which is called Precision Psychiatry. So I connected them to each other. Just send an email. I think you ought to know each other. They got together. I get credit for knowing people and connecting them, but I also benefit them. Leanne needs to raise money. Esther's got money. Esther needs to understand the cutting edge research in depression and biomarkers of depression, which is what Leanne's specialty is, so they benefit. So this is not some icky thing. This is connecting people who benefit from being connected.
turns.zh: 我给学生布置的一个练习是，我会让他们列出10个人，如果你们认识他们，他们也认识你，那么这些人对实现你职业生涯的目标至关重要。比如，如果你想进入生物科技领域，就需要认识10位生物科技行业的高管。列出这10个人后，再想办法与他们建立联系。顺便说一句，不一定非要在社交活动上认识他们。或许你可以效仿约翰·利维（John Levy）的做法，举办晚宴。值得一提的是，晚宴上的客人会亲自下厨，这是一个非常有趣的创意。这种做法恰恰利用了"宜家效应"——人们往往更喜欢自己参与创造的事物。或许你想举办晚宴，或许想在午餐时主动联系他们。（00:36:21）或许你想发送邮件，推荐一篇他们感兴趣的文章，或是介绍一位值得结识的人士。最近，我在社交方面做得还算不错，但比起某些人还是差强人意。最近我结识了埃丝特·沃伊奇基（Esther Wojcicki），我肯定把她的名字念错了。她被誉为硅谷的祖母，是苏珊·沃伊奇基（Susan Wojcicki）的母亲。她对抑郁症，尤其是青少年抑郁症很感兴趣。我建议她认识莱恩·威廉姆斯（Leanne Williams），后者在精神病学与行为科学系工作，发表了约300篇抑郁症相关论文，还开发了名为"精准精神病学"的技术。我帮他们牵线搭桥，只需发送一封邮件。我觉得他们应该认识对方。他们见面后，我既因介绍两人而获益，莱恩也需要筹集资金，而埃丝特有资金支持。埃丝特还想了解抑郁症及生物标志物的前沿研究，而这正是莱恩的专长。因此，这种互惠互利的社交并非令人不适之举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That touches on something you teach in the book is, in your networking you want to become a broker, you want to be central. That's kind of what you want to work on. Can you talk a bit about what that means?
turns.zh: 你书中提到，在社交网络中要成为桥梁人物，处于核心地位。这正是你努力的方向。能否谈谈这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, that means you want to connect people. So many people with benefits, and many groups with benefits for being connected, and they're not connected. What does a venture capitalist do? Connects people with ideas to people with money, and takes a fee for doing it. What does an investment banker do? Connects people trying to sell businesses or raise capital with people trying to buy businesses or who have capital. What's a real estate agent do? Connects buyers and sellers of houses. There are all kinds of examples where the person's entire job is connecting people. But even for the people whose job it isn't, you benefit from knowing people. The more people you know, the more things you know. As I sometimes say in my class, if leadership management, call it what you will, is getting things done through other people, it seems like common sense that the more other people you know, the more you'll be able to get done.
turns.zh: 这意味着要为他人牵线搭桥。许多人因联系而受益，许多群体因联系而受益，而他们原本互不相识。风险投资家做什么？将有创意的人与资金对接，并收取费用。投资银行家做什么？将试图出售企业或融资的人与买家或有资金的人对接。房地产经纪人做什么？为买卖双方牵线搭桥。类似例子不胜枚举，核心工作就是连接人。但即便非以此为业的人，也能从人脉中获益。认识的人越多，了解的信息越多。我有时在课堂上说，如果领导力管理（随你怎么称呼）是通过他人达成目标，那么认识越多人，就越能成事，这似乎是常识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As someone that has become central to a lot of things in the product world, and has built a large network as a result of this podcast newsletter, I can tell you a thousand percent. This creates a lot of opportunity and power, you could say in quotes. So I've seen it happen.
turns.zh: 作为在产品领域成为核心人物，并因播客通讯建立了庞大社交网络的人，我可以百分之百地告诉你，这创造了大量机会和权力——用引号来说就是。事实上，我亲眼见证了这一切。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Of course.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Heap, the product analytics solution that shows you everything users do on your digital product, website, mobile product or other digital services. We all know a great digital experience when we see it. It's intuitive, it anticipates your needs, and it makes it easy for you to do your job. If you're trying to build that kind of experience for your users, you need up to date, reliable information about what your users do in your product and why they do it. Want to know how your users behave across platforms, what keeps them coming back, what they're doing that you're not even aware of? Well, I have some great news for you. Heap captures all of this user activity for you automatically, and then gives you definitive answers to all your questions about user behavior in seconds, not weeks. With Heap, it's easy to prioritize the product investments that improve conversion, engagement and retention. Visit heap.io/Lenny to get started with a demo. That's H-E-A-P dot I-O slash Lenny. (00:40:10): Another lesson I guess you teach is to pursue weak ties. Talk a bit about what that means. What do you mean by that?
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Heap 赞助。Heap 是一款产品分析解决方案，能让您全面了解用户在您的数字产品、网站、移动应用或其他数字服务中的行为。我们都知道优质的数字体验是什么样子——它直观易用，能预测用户需求，帮助用户高效完成工作。若您想为用户打造这样的体验，就需要获取准确、实时的用户行为数据，了解用户在产品中的操作动机。想了解用户跨平台的行为特征、促使他们持续回访的因素，以及那些未被察觉的隐藏需求？现在我有个好消息要告诉您——Heap 能自动捕捉所有用户行为，并在数秒内为您解答关于用户行为的所有疑问，而非等待数周。借助 Heap，您可以轻松优先推进能提升转化率、用户参与度和留存率的产品优化。访问 heap.io/Lenny 即可开始试用，网址是 H-E-A-P 点 I-O，再加一个斜杠和 Lenny。（00:40:10）：我猜您教的另一个技巧是发展弱连接。能否谈谈这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, the people to whom you are strongly tied, your family, your spouse, significant other, your friends, the people who work with you at work will probably, because they are close to you, know the same things and the same people that you do. So to the extent that you build ties with people who are more different from you in every dimension, you are more likely to learn non-redundant information, and come in contact with people that you don't already know. This again seems common sense. There's a lot of research behind it. Mark Granovetter, a sociologist who still teaches at Stanford, wrote a book entitled The Strength of Weak Ties. (00:40:59): And basically, no, actually, pardon me. He wrote an article called The Strength of Weak Ties. His book was called Getting a Job. And he did a study, I guess it was at that time in Boston. He did a study of job seekers in Massachusetts, and he looked at people who got jobs through applying to ads, through more formal means. And then he looked at people who got jobs through referrals from their network. And it turns out, of course, the jobs that you get through your network referrals are much better jobs. And oftentimes the best jobs that people got were referred to them by people that were not particularly close to them. Because they had a view, that's the word I was looking for, a view into the ecosystem of the Boston labor market, that the other people didn't have because they weren't in the same place as the other people.
turns.zh: 嗯，与您关系紧密的人——家人、配偶、重要他人、朋友、同事——往往会因为亲近关系，了解与您相似的人和事。因此，建立与各方面都与您差异较大的人际关系，能让您获取更多非冗余信息，并接触到未知人群。这看似显而易见，但背后有大量研究支持。斯坦福大学在职教授马克·格拉诺维特（Mark Granovetter）曾撰写《弱连接的力量》一书。（00:40:59）：不，准确来说，是一篇名为《弱连接的力量》的文章。他的著作《获得工作的艺术》（Getting a Job）研究了马萨诸塞州求职者的就业情况。研究分两组：一组通过广告投放等正式渠道找到工作，另一组则通过社交网络推荐获得职位。结果发现，网络推荐带来的工作往往更优质，且其中最优质的工作往往来自非亲密关系网的推荐。因为这些人对波士顿劳动力市场的生态有独特见解，而其他人因为身处不同环境，无法获取这些信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that lesson. Let's talk about another power, which is using your power. So when people think of using your power builds more power, that's not intuitive. You talk about how it creates this self-perpetuating growth of power the more you practice power. Can you talk a bit about that?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个观点，再谈谈另一个能力——运用自身权力。当人们认为行使权力会增强权力时，这并不直观。您提到权力越多越能自我强化，能否具体说明一下？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Sure. So when you are given, it's interesting, my friend Deborah Gruenfeld, who wrote a book called Acting with Power, talks a lot about people's ambivalence to power. So sometimes people are put in a job. Herminia Ibarra who teaches now at London Business School, at one point taught in Seattle, at one point taught at Harvard, has an article in the Harvard Business Review in which she talks about a woman in a drug company who gets a promotion, and says to her colleagues, to whom she's now overseeing, that she's not sure why she got the job. She's not sure she deserves the job. Needless to say, she didn't do very well in this job because she got in her own way. But part of this is you are put in a position of power. You're put in a position of authority in order to make things happen. So to the extent you mobilize your resources and get things to happen, you'll get more resources. (00:43:14): People want to be associated with success. To the extent that you become successful, more people will want to work with you. To the extent that you get more stuff done, you'll get more promotions, more opportunities. Nobody's going to give you a job to do if the last five jobs like that they gave you, you couldn't get done. So the more you are able to do, which oftentimes of course requires power and influence, the more you're able to do, the more you'll be asked to do. But better yet, the more resources you'll be given to help you get things done.
turns.zh: 好的。说到这里，我的朋友黛博拉·格鲁恩菲尔德（Deborah Gruenfeld）写了一本叫《权力行动》（Acting with Power）的书，她在书中详细探讨了人们对权力的矛盾心理。比如，有时候人们被赋予某个职位后，会因为不确定自己是否配得上这个职位而犹豫不决。赫米尼亚·伊巴拉（Herminia Ibarra）现在在伦敦商学院任教，曾在西雅图和哈佛大学执教。她在《哈佛商业评论》上发表的一篇文章，讲述了一位制药公司女性获得晋升后，向下属汇报时坦言自己不确定为何能胜任这个职位，甚至怀疑自己是否配得上这份工作。结果她在这份工作中表现不佳，因为她自我设限了。但本质上，当你被赋予权力时，你需要用权力来推动事情进展。只要你能调动资源、促成目标达成，就会获得更多资源。（00:43:14）人们希望与成功者为伍。只要你取得成功，愿意与你共事的人就会增多。只要你能把事情做成，就会获得晋升和更多机会。如果你过去五次类似的工作都未能完成，就没人会再给你这样的机会了。所以，你越能胜任工作，往往就越需要权力和影响力来达成目标。反过来，你获得的资源越多，能完成的任务就越多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think there's interestingly you teach that just showing that you have power creates more power. People see that you have this power and they start to follow your lead more, right? That's a part of this.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你提到只要展示出自己有权力，就能获得更多权力。人们看到你有这种权力，就会更愿意追随你，对吧？这也是其中的一个关键点。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yep. I just saw over the weekend the movie, the latest movie in the franchise of the Planet of the Apes. When Jim Collins left Stanford, he gave me a book called Chimpanzee Politics, which is of course not based on the Planet of the Apes, but it's based upon the study of chimpanzees. We are the same. People are attracted to power, you know that. By the way, that will account for a lot of what is going to happen in the presidential election.
turns.zh: 是的。上周末我刚看了《猩球崛起》系列最新电影。吉姆·柯林斯离开斯坦福大学时，送给我一本《黑猩猩政治》。这本书当然不是基于《猩球崛起》系列电影，而是基于对黑猩猩的研究。我们本质上是一样的。人们被权力吸引，这一点你很清楚。顺便说一句，这将很大程度上影响总统选举的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's save that for the end, because I think that's an interesting piece of your book, of the connection to Trump. So let's save that for a bit. I think that'll be really interesting. Kind of along the same lines of the area we're just talking about. And another rule of power is to show up in a powerful fashion. So look powerful, talk about what that looks like.
turns.zh: 我们先不谈这个，因为我觉得这部分内容与特朗普的关联很有意思，留到最后再说。不过我觉得这与我们刚刚讨论的领域很相契合。还有一条权力法则，就是要以强势姿态亮相。要看起来强大，并解释这种姿态的含义。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: So my colleague at Berkeley, Dana Carney, C-A-R-N-E-Y, is writing a book called Tell, which is about the importance of body language and how to master body language. There is some evidence that suggests we respond mostly to how people look, secondarily to how they sound, and by far the least important to the content of what they say. You can see this by turning on your TV and turning off the sound. Watch the presidential debates with the sound off. They'll be much better. I have another colleague in marketing by the name of Baba Shiv, who talks about people's freaky mind, or the idea that we are in fact descended from primates, and that we are controlled in lots of ways by our emotions. And so we respond affectively to other people. We respond to how they look. There's evidence in economics that suggests tall people earn more salaries, control, earn more money, controlling for lots of things, attractive people. (00:45:46): As long as you're not too attractive, you earn more money. Optimal level of attractiveness because people respond subconsciously to how people look, how they sound, how they show up, how they present themselves. In my class, I take the example of Tony Hayward of BP, the Macondo oil spill, and Lloyd Blankfein who was accused of shorting the securities that he was selling, which by the way, Goldman did. And before I let them hear Tony or Lloyd, we show about 60 seconds. And Lloyd's case 34 seconds with no sound. And even if you did not know who these people were and I asked you to make a bet, who's going to keep their job and who's going to lose it? You would know just from their physical appearance.
turns.zh: 我的伯克利同事达娜·卡尼（Dana Carney）正在写一本名为《Tell》的书，书中探讨了肢体语言的重要性以及如何掌握肢体语言。一些研究表明，我们对人的外表印象最深刻，其次是说话声线，而说话内容的重要性则最低。你可以通过打开电视但关掉声音来验证这一点——关掉声音观看总统辩论会的效果会好得多。我还有一位市场营销领域的同事巴巴·希夫（Baba Shiv），他谈到人们的"奇特心理"，即我们实际上是从灵长类动物进化而来的，并且在很多方面受情绪控制。因此，我们会根据他人的外表和语气做出情感反应。经济学研究表明，身高较高的人收入更高，掌控力更强——当然，这是在控制其他因素的情况下——长相漂亮的人同样如此。（00:45:46）只要你不是特别漂亮，你就能赚更多钱。吸引力的最佳水平在于人们会下意识地根据外表、语气和表现来做出判断。在我的课堂上，我以英国石油公司（BP）的托尼·海沃德（Tony Hayward）和麦康度石油泄漏事件为例，还有被指控卖空自己所售证券的劳埃德·布兰克芬（Lloyd Blankfein）——顺便说一句，高盛公司也曾卷入其中。在播放相关片段前，我先给学生们看一段60秒的视频。劳埃德的案例只有34秒，且无声音。即便你不知道这些人是谁，让你猜测谁能保住职位、谁会下台，你也能仅凭他们的外表判断出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: And by the way, what Dana Carney will tell you, and what common sense will tell you, is that these are skills that can be mastered. Robert de Niro was not born Robert de Niro, in the sense of acting skills are learned. How you show up, how you command the room. There's a guy named Regis McKenna who is older than God, who's famous for running a very, very, very fancy public relations firm in the Silicon Valley. And his biggest contribution to life, as well as by the way to his personal wealth, is that he made Steve Jobs Steve Jobs. When Steve Jobs began, Steve Jobs couldn't convince you to buy water if you were dying of thirst. He could not give a presentation to save his life. And Regis McKenna and his team took Steve Jobs under their wing and created Steve Jobs, a man who could sell anything to anybody. These are skills. This is not about personality. This is not about undergoing some kind of cosmetic surgery or whatever. These are skills, everything we've talked about, networking, showing up, all these things. These are skills that can be learned.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，达娜·卡尼会告诉你，常识也会告诉你，这些都是可以掌握的技能。罗伯特·德尼罗并非天生就是罗伯特·德尼罗——演技是后天习得的。如何在人群中展现自信，如何掌控局面。有位叫雷吉斯·麦肯纳（Regis McKenna）的人（他比上帝还年长），因在硅谷经营一家极其高端的公关公司而闻名。他对生活乃至个人财富的最大贡献，就是把史蒂夫·乔布斯打造成史蒂夫·乔布斯。当史蒂夫·乔布斯刚起步时，即便你口渴得要死，他也无法说服你买水。他连做个推销都难如登天。雷吉斯·麦肯纳及其团队接纳了史蒂夫·乔布斯，成功将他打造成一个能向任何人推销任何东西的人。这些都是技巧——而非性格特征，也不是整容手术之类的。这些都是可以习得的技能——我们讨论的所有内容：社交、展现自我，诸如此类。这些都是可以掌握的技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a list of some of the stuff you actually recommend for looking and appearing powerful. So I'll read a few and I'm curious what else comes to mind. So do not read from notes. Make eye contact. Keep it brief. You say that anger can be a signal of power because it's outside the norm. It's kind of breaking the rules. Don't apologize. It's kind of the opposite. More gestures, which is interesting. Open body posture. Louder voice. Okay, I'm going to speak louder now. I like this. Okay, what else comes to mind as ways to appear powerful?
turns.zh: 我列了一些能让你看起来强大有力的建议。让我读几条，然后看看你们还能想到什么。别照着笔记念。保持眼神接触。时间要简短。愤怒可以传递权力感，因为它超出常规，是种打破规则的行为。别道歉，恰恰相反。多做手势，这挺有趣的。保持开放的肢体姿势。提高音量。好的，我现在要大声点说话了。我喜欢这样。好的，还能想到什么能让人看起来强大的方法？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Invading people's personal space. So gentle touching, standing close to someone. We're not talking about sexual touching, we're talking touch on the arm or the shoulder, shaking people's hands. That's a way of I think being more powerful. But you've covered the main ones. Eye contact. One of the problems with Tony Hayward of BP is that he's been given a statement to read. You cannot read something in front of you and make eye contact at the same time. So he looks like he's scripted. He looks like he's insincere. Jack Valenti, who I had the privilege of knowing, who for 38 years was the head of the Motion Picture Association of America, and typically rated one of the number one or number two most effective lobbyists in Washington DC, said to my class when he came to my class, which he did, "I never appeared before Congress with notes. I wanted them to believe, which was by the way, true, that I was in complete control and complete mastery of the material, and that I did not need notes or a bunch of assistants around me to help me. (00:49:40): That I, as the head of the MPAA, understood the motion picture industry." And then he would give you a little aside about how it was the one industry that consistently had a budget surplus in trade. He would talk about how many jobs he created and he had all this stuff at his fingertips. But basically his command of the material made him more powerful. It's interesting, Jack Valenti was five foot two inches tall and he came, talked to my class, and the next class I said to people, "What are your reactions? What are your thoughts?" And a woman raised her hand and said, "He feels taller than he is." And I thought that was an assessment that was both true and insightful. When the five-foot-two Jack Valenti appeared, because of his presence, because of his body language, because of his Texas drawl, because of how he moved on the stage, he felt bigger. You would not say he did not feel five-foot-two.
turns.zh: 侵犯他人个人空间。比如轻柔的触碰、站得太近。当然，我们说的不是性接触，而是手臂或肩膀的轻触、握手之类的。我认为这些举动能彰显一个人的自信。不过你已经讲到了主要的几点——眼神交流。英国石油公司（BP）的托尼·海沃德（Tony Hayward）就曾遇到过这个问题，他被要求照着事先准备好的发言稿念稿。这样一来，你就无法同时保持眼神交流，看起来就像在照本宣科，显得不真诚。我有幸结识的杰克·瓦伦蒂（Jack Valenti）曾担任美国电影协会（MPAA）主席38年，他被公认为华盛顿特区最具影响力的游说者之一。他来给我们上课时曾说：“我从不带着讲稿去国会。我想让他们相信——顺便说一句，这是真心的——我完全掌控局面，精通相关内容，无需笔记或助手帮忙。作为MPAA的主席，我深知电影行业的运作规律。”接着他会顺便提及，电影行业是唯一一个贸易顺差持续稳定的行业。他会谈及创造了多少就业岗位，信手拈来各种数据。但归根结底，他对业务的精通让他显得更加强大。有趣的是，身高仅5英尺2英寸的杰克·瓦伦蒂出场时给人一种高大威猛的感觉——无论是仪态、肢体语言，还是得克萨斯州特有的拖腔，都让人觉得他比实际身高更高大。此外，舞台上的表现力也让他显得格外自信。人们不会觉得他身高只有5英尺2英寸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me read a couple more because this is a good example of stuff he did. Other ways to appear more powerful is more speaking time, longer gazing time, more disinhibited laughs. Is that just you laughing and feeling like you're just...
turns.zh: 接下来我想再讲几个例子，因为这是他做事的典型手法。其他增强气场的手段包括：增加发言时间、延长注视时长、更随意地大笑。就是那种你笑着却又感觉自己只是……

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Well, humor. Humor. The famous author, Salman Rushdie said, and I quote Salman Rushdie, it's a fabulous quote. "If you can get people to laugh, you can tell them anything."
turns.zh: 嗯，幽默。著名作家萨尔曼·鲁西迪（Salman Rushdie）说过一句妙语，我引用一下：“如果你能让人们开怀大笑，就能让他们相信任何事情。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, stand-up comedy is a great example that. So again, I think here people might be hearing this and they're like, I don't want to be this person. I don't want to be talking all the time. I don't want to be pretending like open posture. Is the advice here just you don't need to do all these things. Just know this makes people more powerful. Don't necessarily judge people, do some of these things maybe because it'll add to your power? How do you think about just people that are turned off by this sort of thing?
turns.zh: 是啊，比如单口喜剧就是个很好的例子。所以我觉得听众可能会想，我不想成为这样的人。我不想一直说话。我不想假装姿态开放。你的建议是说不必做这些事，只要明白这些举动能增强个人影响力就行了？但人们对这些行为反感怎么办？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: That's a wonderful question. So I say to my class, on the very first day of class, that we will go through four stages. We'll go through the stage of denial. It doesn't work in my culture, it doesn't work in my organization, doesn't work for me, it doesn't work in my religion, whatever. Then we'll go through anger. When they get angry at me, how can you teach us this stuff? Then they'll go into sadness. I actually believe this and I'm depressed. And if we're successful, they will go through acceptance. And the process I have, again, I do not have the most popular class at Stanford Business School because I am good-looking, because I'm the smartest person at Stanford or anything else. I am strategic about thinking about if I have someone who's going to come into this class, I have to get them from denial to acceptance in 10 weeks. (00:52:38): And how are we going to do that? The easiest way to do that, if I said, Lenny, I want you to become a better tennis player, or a better roller blader, or a better ice skater, whatever, a better piano player in 10 weeks, what would we do? If we have practice and coaching. And that's what I do in the class, practice and coaching. I have executive coaches who work with the class and I give them assignments that ask them to practice what they're learning. And therefore, by the end of the class, most people have made this transition because it is true. If you've never... I had a dinner the other night, this Israeli woman who's like, I've done amazing stuff. Amazing. Which is fabulous. And she said at the dinner, she said, "I would've never done this before taking your class." And the way you get them to do this is I don't say, Lenny, you're going to swim the English Channel tomorrow. (00:53:38): If I want you to swim the English Channel, we're going to start by swimming in pools and make every day a little bit more challenging. That's what we do. I don't start by saying, you're going to network like Keith Ferrazzi or John Levy, or you're not going to be as bold as Jason Calacanis, who trust me is extraordinarily bold. You're not going to necessarily do what I did. You're going to begin where you can begin, and push yourself out of your comfort zone. Because, and again, this is common sense. (00:54:13): There's also a ton of research behind it. If you always stay in your comfort zone, you'll never do anything different or better than what you're currently doing. This is true. If I said to you, I want you to, at the end of 10 weeks, lift a hundred pounds, I can't do that by on the last day saying lift a hundred pounds. We have to work up to it. And that is, it's the same principle here. So don't do something that looks so off the wall or so out of character for you that you can't conceive doing it. Push yourself a little, push yourself a little.
turns.zh: 这是个很棒的问题。所以我在课程的第一天就告诉学生，我们将经历四个阶段。首先是"否认阶段"。在我的文化中，这行不通；在我的组织里，这行不通；对我个人而言，这行不通；在我的宗教信仰中，这行不通等等。接下来是"愤怒阶段"。当他们对我发火时——你怎么能教我们这些东西？——然后他们会进入"悲伤阶段"。我真的相信这一点，但我感到沮丧。如果我们成功了，他们就会进入"接受阶段"。我再次强调，我在斯坦福商学院的课程并非最受欢迎的，不是因为我长得帅，也不是因为我是斯坦福最聪明的人之类的。而是因为我深思熟虑地考虑：如果有人来上我的课，我必须在10周内让他们从否认阶段过渡到接受阶段。（00:52:38）那要怎么做呢？最简单的方法，如果我对你说，"莱尼，我想让你在10周内成为更出色的网球选手、轮滑者、滑冰者，或者钢琴家"，我们该怎么做？答案是训练和指导。在我的课程中，我就是这样做的——训练和指导。我有执行教练与学生合作，还布置让他们实践所学内容的作业。因此，到课程结束时，大多数人都完成了这种转变，因为这是事实。如果你从未……前几天我参加了一场晚宴，一位以色列女性说，我做过惊人的事。太棒了。她在晚宴上说道："上你的课之前，我绝不会做这些事。"而让他们做到这些事的方法不是说："莱尼，你明天要游过英吉利海峡。"（00:53:38）如果我想让你游过英吉利海峡，我们会从在泳池游泳开始，每天都增加难度。这才是我们该做的。我不会说："你要像基思·费拉齐或约翰·利维那样社交"，或者"你要像杰森·卡拉卡尼斯那样大胆"——相信我，他确实非常大胆。你不必非要效仿我。你要从自己能做到的地方开始，然后不断突破舒适区。因为，这又是个常识。（00:54:13）对此也有大量研究支持。如果你一直待在舒适区，你永远无法做出与现状不同或更出色的事情。这是事实。如果我对你说："10周后你要举起100磅重物"，我不可能在最后一天直接让你举起100磅。我们必须逐步达成目标。这里也是同样的道理。所以别做那些看起来太离谱或太不符合你性格的事。稍微挑战一下自己，稍微挑战一下自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's an interesting connection here too. What some say is kind of the opposite of your class at Stanford, which is Touchy-Feely. We had Carole Robin on the podcast and she has a framework, the 15% rule where you push yourself 15% beyond your comfort zone. Where it's just a little bit, but it's not too far, and it feels like you try to do a similar thing.
turns.zh: 这里还有个有趣的关联。有些人说这和斯坦福的"感性课程"正好相反。我们在播客上邀请过卡罗尔·罗宾，她提出了一个框架——15%规则，即挑战自己，超越舒适区15%。虽然只是一点点，但又不会太过分，让人感觉自己在努力做类似的事。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So you begin by doing what you don't think you can do.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。所以你从做自己认为做不到的事开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's spend a little more time here around the homework assignments, and this kind of Knowing-Doing Gap that you talked about. So you shared a couple of homework assignments you give already, find 10 people, think of 10 people you want to meet that'll help you with your career and then try to meet them. And then there's this, I guess my friend started a podcast, I don't know which homework it was. What other homework assignments do you give?
turns.zh: 让我们再花点时间讨论一下作业任务，以及你提到的"知行差距"问题。你之前分享过几个作业任务，比如找10个能助力职业发展的潜在人脉，再去拜访他们。还有一个作业任务，我猜是关于播客的，我记不清具体内容了。你还有哪些其他作业任务呢？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: So we begin, there's a literature on goal setting that says if you set goals, you're more likely to achieve them. This is, again, not some huge insight, but there's an enormous scientific literature about this. And so I begin the very first homework assignment is, which is by the way, on the very first day of class, why are you here? Why are you here? It is now the end of this class. What would success look like to you? What would you like to accomplish in our 10 weeks together? Second assignment, I give them a reading from the Power book, which is the book before Seven Rules, which talks about the seven attributes of power. Go out and get people to rate you on these or rate yourself. Set for yourself a development plan, energy, focus, being willing to tolerate conflict, all these qualities. What are you strong on? What are you weak on? What do you want to build during our time together, and how are you going to do it? (00:56:35): So we begin with goal setting. One of the assignments I give them, which is the class that Jason comes to, what resources can you create? You're at Stanford Business School, elite, fancy Stanford. What can you do in your 10 weeks here? I have people who created awards. A woman who created an award gave it to Karlie Kloss, the model. Got in trouble with the school. It turns out it's easier to ask forgiveness than permission. So what can you do to create resources that will give you some leverage? That would be a third assignment. The networking is a fourth assignment. The acting with power. I show them the videos and I tell them in advance of the class, and I tell them they need to become Tony Hayward. They need to do a better job, which is, by the way, a low bar, representing BP. And give me a 60 to 90 second video and then share it with colleagues and get feedback on it. And then we're going to call on people in the class. (00:57:47): In other words, for every idea, I try to think of something. And this is all, by the way, this is all front-loaded. And by the end of the class we're not doing this so much. But I try to give them an exercise that causes them to actually take that idea and implement it. Find people, oh, for branding. Write a personal brand statement, get some feedback on it, then write it again. How do you want to be known? Which is by the way, useful to you because you're a second-year MBA, you're going to go in the job market. What do you want people to think about you? How do you want people to respond to you? How do you want to be known? So I basically take for every topic and have them do it. And then the coach, their person, their coach, who is responsible for 23 of these people, give them feedback on this.
turns.zh: 首先，有关目标设定的文献指出，如果设定了目标，就更有可能实现它们。这并非什么深刻见解，但相关科学研究非常丰富。因此，我布置的第一个作业任务是——顺便说一下，这是在课程的第一天——"你为什么来这里？"现在课程即将结束，你眼中的成功是什么样子？在我们共处的10周里，你希望达成什么目标？第二个作业任务是让学生阅读《权力》一书中的内容（这本书比《七条法则》更早），书中讨论了权力的七个属性。去找人评估你的这些特质，或者自我评估。为自己制定发展计划，包括能量、专注力、容忍冲突的意愿等品质。你的优势是什么？弱点是什么？在共同学习期间，你想培养哪些能力，又该如何实现？（00:56:35）：所以我们从目标设定开始。给杰森所在班级的学生布置的作业是——你们在斯坦福商学院，精英学府，环境优越。在这里10周内能创造什么资源？有学生创建了奖项。有一位女生给超模卡莉·克劳斯颁发奖项，结果惹上麻烦。事实证明，征求许可比请求原谅更容易。所以如何创造资源，获得影响力？这是第三个作业任务。社交网络是第四个作业任务。展示视频并提前告知学生，要扮演托尼·海沃德（BP前CEO）的角色，做好得差一点也行，然后制作60-90秒视频，分享给同事获取反馈。最后在课堂上提问。（00:57:47）：总之，每个主题我都会设想对应的实践活动。所有内容都是前置学习，课程结束后我们会减少这类活动。但我会布置能让学生真正实践的作业。比如品牌塑造，写个人品牌宣言，获得反馈后再修改。如何希望被认知？这对你们很有用，因为你们是MBA二年级生，即将进入职场。希望别人如何看待你？如何回应你？如何被认知？所以每个主题我都会让学生实践。最后由负责23名学生的导师提供反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see how this makes a big impact on someone's life.
turns.zh: 我能感受到这对人们的生活产生了重大影响。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah. And so at the end, I had a student a couple years ago said to me, "It is not that I got more feedback and more useful feedback from your class than I did in any other class. I got more useful feedback in your class than I did on every other class I took combined."
turns.zh: 是啊。所以最后，几年前有个学生对我说：“我从你的课上得到的反馈和有用的建议，比我在其他任何课程中获得的都要多。我在你的课上得到的有用反馈，比我在其他所有课程加起来得到的还要多。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can see why. Let's talk about the last power. So we've talked through six already. We have only one more to go, which is maybe the one that probably upsets people most, which is that once you have power, people will forget what you did to get there. Talk about what that looks like and is that a power or is it more just like this is what you should know about.
turns.zh: 我能理解为什么会这样。让我们来谈谈最后一种权力。到现在我们已经讨论了六种权力了，还剩一种，可能就是最让人不爽的那种——一旦你获得了权力，人们就会忘记你为了获得它付出了什么努力。请谈谈这种情况具体是怎样的，这到底算是一种权力，还是说更应该把它看作是一些你应该了解的常识？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: And I put in rule seven for the following reason. In spite of everything that you and I have been talking about, many people in a stage of, I don't know, denial or something, say, I'm worried that if I do this, at the end... People believe that the world is homeostatic. It is not. That it's going to adjust, but whatever. At the end I will be brought low. They have the myth of Icarus in their head. You fly too close to the sun, your wings are going to melt, you're going to be brought down. And so I try to convince them, partly through a lecture and partly through rule seven. And some of the principles that I talk about in rule seven. That, in fact, life is not homeostatic at all. That life is actually self-fulfilling. If I believe you're powerful, you will become more powerful. (01:00:26): If I believe you have no power, you will wind up with almost no power, and that therefore it is all forgotten and forgiven. And I begin, I believe I begin. But if not, I could begin with the story of the South Carolina Senator who says nasty things about Trump, and then Lindsey Graham, and becomes Trump's biggest acolyte. And the New York Times, of course, is fascinated by this. How can you say all these horrible things about Trump and now be his, basically have your lips affixed to some part of his anatomy? And Lindsey's answer is, I want to be relevant. He's the President of the United States. This goes back to the judgment. I like him, this, that, the other thing. He's the president. If I want to get legislation passed, he, by the way, has taken over the Republican Party. (01:01:22): If I want to get stuff done, I need to have him on my side. And like many narcissists and egomaniacs, it is not a good way to get them on your side by saying nasty things about them. So this is the pragmatics. People forget that Bill Gates stole the code on which Microsoft has built. People forget that Jeffrey Epstein, after being convicted of sex offenses, was still having dinners with members of the royal family and members of the New York media elite. People forget that Martha Stewart, who served time in jail, has a brand that's never been more valuable. People forget all this stuff. (01:02:19): I still remember sitting in the office of someone whose name I won't use, but I'll use enough that if somebody wanted to search it out, you could. So I am sitting in this guy's office and he's, by the way, a Jewish man. He's got pictures of him with the Pope, he's got pictures of him with Ronald Reagan. He's got pictures with him, with all these people. What is his secret? He, by the way, took a company into bankruptcy. People lost literally billions of dollars. He was fined. He lost money, but he walked away with about $700 million. It turns out, $700 million makes you a big deal. Lives at the biggest house in Los Angeles or one of the biggest houses in Los Angeles. I can't keep up with the construction of the big houses. People want to be close to money, power, and success, and they will overlook your flaws to be close to you.
turns.zh: 接下来，我之所以制定了第七条规则，是出于以下原因。尽管你我一直在探讨这些问题，但许多人仍处于一种——我不知道该如何形容的——否认现状的阶段。他们会说：“我担心如果我这么做，最终……” 人们总以为世界是恒定不变的。但事实并非如此。世界会自我调整，但无论如何，最终我都会被打倒。他们脑中充斥着伊卡洛斯神话——你飞得太近太阳，翅膀会被烧化，最终坠落。因此，我试图说服他们——一部分通过讲座，一部分通过第七条规则——以及我在这条规则中所阐述的某些原则。事实上，生命根本就不是恒定不变的。生命本质上是自我实现的。如果你相信自己强大，你就会变得更强大；如果你认为自己无能为力，最终你将一无所有。因此，我开始行动，我相信自己已经行动了。但如果没有行动，我可以从南卡罗来纳州参议员的故事讲起。他曾对特朗普恶语相向，后来却成了特朗普最忠实的追随者。《纽约时报》对此倍感兴趣：你怎么能说特朗普那么坏，现在却又巴结他呢？林赛·格雷厄姆的回答是：“我想保持相关性。” 特朗普是美国总统。这又回到了判断力的问题。我喜欢他，喜欢他这个人，喜欢他做的其他事。但他毕竟是总统。如果我想推动立法，他已经接管了共和党。（01:01:22）如果我想办成事，就必须拉拢他。像许多自恋狂和利己主义者一样，用恶语相向来拉拢他们可不是明智之举。所以这就是务实主义。人们忘记了比尔·盖茨窃取了微软赖以建立的代码。人们忘记了杰弗里·爱泼斯坦被判性犯罪后，仍与王室成员和纽约媒体精英共进晚餐。人们忘记了玛莎·斯图尔特入狱服刑后，其品牌价值却空前高涨。人们忘记了所有这些事。（01:02:19）我还记得坐在某人的办公室里——我不会透露他的名字，但如果你想查证，足以找到——那个人顺便说，是个犹太人。他和教皇的合影，和罗纳德·里根的合影，还有其他名人的合影。他的秘诀是什么？顺便说一句，他曾让一家公司破产。人们损失了数十亿美元。他被罚款，失去了财富，但最终带走约7亿美元。原来7亿美元就能让你变得举足轻重。他住在洛杉矶最大的房子里，或者说最大之一。我跟不上豪宅建设的步伐。人们渴望接近金钱、权力和成功，他们会忽视你的缺点，只为接近你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, you talk about this in the book. You're not describing how the world should work. This is just how it is, and this is how you can be successful in the world that we live in.
turns.zh: 再说一次，你在书中也谈到这些。你不是在描述世界应该如何运作。这就是现实，而这也是我们所处的世界中如何取得成功的法则。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: And by the way, this is how the world not only is, but how it was and how it will be. Because these ideas are not something that I sat down one day and made up or something. These ideas, everything that I talk about, including this last one, has social science and logic behind it. So you can explain not only what is, but why it is.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，世界不仅是现在这个样子，过去如此，未来也将如此。因为这些观点并非我某天突发奇想编造出来的。我所谈论的一切，包括最后提到的这些观点，都基于社会科学和逻辑推理。因此，你不仅能解释事物的现状，还能揭示其背后的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, let's talk about Trump for a bit. At the beginning of your book, you say that basically you were going to write a book about why Trump is so successful and what he's done so well. And your realization is no one's going to pay attention if here's how to be like Trump. And essentially, if you think about all these rules, it's clear he is very good at all of these things.
turns.zh: 那么，让我们稍微谈谈特朗普。在你的书开头，你说你原本打算写一本关于特朗普为何如此成功以及他做得好的地方的书。但后来你意识到，如果你教人们如何效仿特朗普，没人会感兴趣。仔细想想这些规则，很明显他在所有这些方面都非常擅长。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: That's correct. By the way, not because he read the book, but because he does it through trial and error or something.
turns.zh: 没错。顺便说一句，不是因为他读了那本书，而是通过不断尝试和犯错学会的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when people hear that, they're like, I don't want to be Trump. I don't like how Trump is. I don't want to be seen that way. Do you have any thoughts on just how to make people feel comfortable following some of these powers and building power, knowing that, oh wow, maybe he's the epitome of some of this stuff?
turns.zh: 所以当人们听到这些时，他们会说，我不想成为特朗普。我不喜欢特朗普的行事方式。我不想被这样看待。对于如何让人们安心遵循这些权力法则并积累权力，你有什么想法吗？毕竟，特朗普或许是其中某些特质的典型代表。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: I will tell you a story. In 1993, a woman named Laura Esserman, who's a doctor, took my class. She claims publicly that this is the only class at Stanford for which she did all the reading. By the way, while she was getting her MBA at Stanford, she was having her first child and practicing medicine full time. Laura Esserman said to me one day, "You have a case. You have cases on all these people doing evil things. Why don't you ever write a case about somebody doing good things?" And of course, I wrote a case about her. So she comes to the class. Case was published in probably 2003, 2004. (01:05:31): She comes to the class and the students are, what is the right word? Hard on her? That would be a modest thing. The students eviscerate her because she is incredibly smart, incredibly well-intentioned, but she will not network. She says, "I don't have time for schmoozing." She will not do almost any of the stuff that we talk about today. So she and her husband, Michael Endicott, two of my closest friends in the world, and I go out to lunch afterwards. And smoke is coming out of her ears and she is pissed off. And this is a very accomplished woman and a very smart woman. And she's pissed. I said to her, "Laura, you have boundless energy and boundless intelligence. You're a force of nature. Let me discuss something from the past subject of physics. (01:06:39): You are creating friction. With enough force you can overcome the friction. If you reduce the friction, just think how much more you could accomplish." And she looked at me and changed. And I will tell you, and I've said this publicly, because I get to introduce her for all the awards she's won, and she's now won a ton of them. Including Time Magazine 2016 list of a hundred most influential people in the world. And I say to people, and I say it with pride, that of all the things I've done in my life, the thing I'm most proud of and most proud of is creating Laura Esserman.
turns.zh: 我要讲个故事。1993年，斯坦福大学的一位女博士生劳拉·埃瑟曼来上我的课。她公开声称，这是斯坦福唯一一门她完整读完所有案例的课程。顺便说一句，当时她在斯坦福攻读MBA学位时，正怀着第一个孩子，同时还要全职行医。有一天，劳拉对我说：“你有一个案例。所有做坏事的人都有案例。为什么你从不写一个做好事的人的案例？”当然，我为她写了一个案例。于是她来上课。案例大概在2003年或2004年出版。（01:05:31）：她来上课时，学生们对她可不友好。用一个委婉的说法就是“对她不太友好”。学生们把她批得体无完肤，因为她极其聪明，出发点极好，但她不善于社交。她说：“我没时间去寒暄。”她几乎不做我们今天讨论的所有事情。课后，我和她的丈夫迈克尔·恩迪科特（我世上最亲密的两个朋友）一起出去吃午饭。她怒气冲冲，烟从耳朵里冒出来。这位才华横溢、极具智慧的女性，满腔怒火。我对她说：“劳拉，你精力充沛，智慧过人。你是个天生的强者。我来谈谈物理学的旧课题。（01:06:39）你正在制造摩擦。只要有足够的力量就能克服摩擦。如果减少摩擦，想想你能成就多大的事业。”她看着我，改变了态度。我要告诉你们，我公开说过这事，因为我要为她赢得的所有奖项做介绍，她现在获奖无数，包括《时代》杂志2016年度全球最具影响力人物榜单。我对人们说，我一生中最引以为傲的事，就是造就了劳拉·埃瑟曼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome story and a really good way of thinking about this from a different angle.
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的故事，也是从不同角度思考这个问题的好方法。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah, no, and I said to Laura, I said, "You want to make profound changes in the drug development process. You want to make profound changes in whether or not we learn from the treatments that are being given to people. You want to make profound changes in the connection between research and teaching, research and practice. You want to do all these things. If you are going to accomplish any of these things, you need to cross the bridge." And she hasn't crossed the bridge completely and she and I joke about it. But she crossed the bridge a lot and she has accomplished incredible things. She's won every cancer award that can be given. And by the way, she's won all these awards for the American Cancer Society, who she fought with. She's won these awards from the Susan Cohen Foundation, who she fought with.
turns.zh: 是啊，不行。我对劳拉说，我说：“你想对药物研发过程进行深刻变革。你想彻底改变我们能否从现有治疗中吸取经验的现状。你想打通科研与教学、科研与实践之间的桥梁。你想做所有这些事。如果你想实现其中任何一项，就必须跨越这座桥。”她还没完全跨过这座桥，我们常拿这事开玩笑。但她确实跨过了很多桥，取得了令人惊叹的成就。她赢得了所有能获得的癌症奖项。顺便说一句，她还为美国癌症协会赢得了奖项——而她曾与该协会存在分歧。她还获得了苏珊·科恩基金会的奖项——而她也曾与该基金会产生过冲突。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is an incredible example of the opening quote to your book that I have here. "If you want power to be used for good, more good people need to have power."
turns.zh: 这是我手头这本书开篇引语的一个绝佳例子。“如果你想让权力用于善事，就必须让更多善良的人掌握权力。”

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: That's exactly right.
turns.zh: 说得太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I like the, it's like a quote attributed to me, is how you...
turns.zh: 我喜欢这句话，这句话好像是引用我说的，是这样的。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I don't remember saying it, but somebody said, I said it. I'll take credit for it. I said to Laura, "You want to change medicine? Medicine is not going to change without the application of power and influence." If change was going to happen, it would've happened already. You have to take on entrenched interests. She has a whole thing, which we need not go into because it's pretty technical, on screening. She said, everybody's getting a mammogram every year beyond a certain age, which is stupid for a variety of reasons. You can read, she was on the PBS NewsHour about this. This is what got her in trouble with the radiologists. The radiologists, of course, are selling screening. She said, there's some people that need to be screened every month, and there's some people that need to be screened never because of their genetics. She wants custom tailored screening or precision screening. Anyway, she fights everybody. (01:09:29): Richard Blum, Dianne Feinstein's husband, both Dianne and Richard Blum are now deceased, was at a thing where she launched the Athena Project. The Athena Project, she's now, with her collaborators, collecting data on the diagnosis and treatment and outcome for 150,000 patients in the University of California Healthcare System. So I'm supposed to give some opening talk to provide entertainment. And Dick Blum is there. Dick Blum, of course is wealthy. He's Dianne Feinstein's husband. I said to him, "Dick, how did Laura get you here?" And I still remember, I think this is a quote in one of the books I wrote. He said to me, he said, "Look." He said, "I've learned that at the end of the day when Laura asks you to do something, you may say no, but at the end of the day, you're going to do it anyway. Save yourself the aggravation."
turns.zh: 是啊。不过我不记得自己说过这话，但有人说是我说的，我认了。我对劳拉说：“你想改变医学？没有权力和影响力的应用，医学就不会改变。”如果变革要发生的话，早就该发生了。你必须对抗根深蒂固的既得利益。她在筛查方面有一整套理论，我们暂且不深究，因为这太专业了。她说，超过一定年龄的人每年都要做乳腺 X 光检查，这在很多方面都是愚蠢的。你可以去读相关资料，她曾就此事上过 PBS 新闻一小时节目。这就是她和放射科医生产生矛盾的原因。放射科医生当然在大力推销筛查。她说，有些人需要每月筛查一次，有些人因为基因原因永远不需要筛查。她主张个性化筛查或精准筛查。总之，她处处与人抗争。（01:09:29）：理查德·布鲁姆，黛安·范斯坦的丈夫，黛安和理查德如今都已离世。他出席了她启动雅典娜计划的活动。雅典娜计划中，她与合作伙伴正在收集加州大学医疗系统中 15 万名患者的诊断、治疗和治疗结果数据。我本该做开场致辞活跃气氛。理查德·布鲁姆也在场。理查德当然很富有。他是黛安·范斯坦的丈夫。我对他说：“理查德，劳拉怎么把你请来的？”我至今记得，我写的某本书里引用过这句话。他说：“看吧。”他说：“我发现，当劳拉让你做事时，你可以说不，但到头来你还是会照做。省得自己生气。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I feel like you're just endlessly full of good stories that we could just keep going on and on. Let me try to summarize the rules of power real quick and see if anything else emerges. And then have just a couple more questions. So the Seven Rules of Power, get out of your own way, break the rules, show up in a powerful fashion, create a powerful brand, network relentlessly, use your power, and understand that once you've acquired power, that what you did to get there will be forgiven, forgotten, or both. Let me ask you a question, maybe half in jest. You teach people how to acquire power. Why aren't you the most powerful man in the world?
turns.zh: 天哪，我感觉你简直有说不完的精彩故事，听得我们欲罢不能。让我快速总结一下权力法则，看看能否挖掘出更多内涵。然后再问几个问题。七条权力法则是：摆脱自我束缚、打破规则、以强势姿态亮相、打造强大品牌、坚持不懈建立人脉、运用权力，以及一旦获取权力，你为达此目的所采取的手段要么被原谅，要么被遗忘，要么两者兼有。容我冒昧一问——你教人如何获取权力，可你自己为什么不是世界上最有权势的人呢？

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Ah, that's a very good question. To which I have a very good answer. I have a colleague who's unfortunately now deceased, by the name of James G. March, who was a very, very distinguished scholar. And James March said to me many, many years ago, something which is completely true. You can have power or you can have autonomy, but you cannot have both. And I have chosen to live a life of freedom, autonomy. I could tell you stories that would bring tears to your eyes. I'll tell you one. We had a dean of the Business School whose wife was dying of cancer, and she was projected to die in the fall. So the Business School goes to him and says, we'll give you the fall off to be with your wife. She lives until June. It's now winter. (01:11:46): You have responsibilities as the Dean of the Business School. You have to meet with alumni. You have to go around and raise money. You have to show up at events, university events. I do not necessarily think that is how he wanted to spend the winter and spring quarters, but that's what you have to do. When I wanted Jack Valenti to come to my class, I did not call Jack Valenti. I called Judy Dickey. Judy Dickey was his assistant. Judy Dickey controlled his schedule. I meet Jack on such and such a day. He can't make it on that day. Fine. I can adjust the schedule. Can he make it on this day? (01:12:24): When I wanted my friend Gary Loveman, who ran Harrah's and Caesars and then was the number two executive at Aetna, I want him to come to my class. I called Reggie Kirk. I didn't call Gary Loveman. And that's all you need to know. I do not have an assistant who controls my schedule. I control my schedule. You will not find my Outlook calendar on any website, on any computer. I want autonomy. If I said to you, "Lenny, I will give you $1 billion, or for that matter, $10 billion if you can buy-"
turns.zh: 嗯，这确实是个好问题。我对此有个绝佳的答案。我有一位已故的同事叫詹姆斯·G·马奇，他是位极负盛名的学者。多年前，他曾对我说一句至理名言：你要么拥有权力，要么享有自主权，但二者不可兼得。我选择了自由自主的生活。说起这方面，我能讲出许多令人动容的故事。比如，我们商学院一位院长的妻子患癌症，预计秋季离世。学院找他说：秋季学期你可以请假陪妻子。但她活到了六月份，而此时已是冬季。（01:11:46）作为院长，你得履行职责——接待校友、筹款、出席各类活动。这些事务可不是他想度过冬春两季的方式。但职责所在必须完成。当我想请杰克·瓦伦蒂来上课时，我没直接联系他，而是找了他的助理朱迪·迪基。朱迪掌控着他的日程安排。我约定某天见面，他那天有事无法到场？没关系，我可以调整日期。改到另一天行不行？（01:12:24）还有想请加里·洛夫曼来上课，他曾执掌哈拉斯和凯撒娱乐集团，后来又担任安泰保险二号人物。我联系了雷吉·柯克，从不打给洛夫曼本人。你懂的，这就是关键所在。我没有助理来管控日程，都是我自己安排。Outlook日历不会出现在任何网站或电脑上。我要自主权。如果你问我：“伦尼，要是能给你10亿美元，甚至100亿美元，你就能买到——”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: Wait, if you can have last week again. You can't. You can't. Time goes in only one direction. I want control of my time. It is much more important to me, being a Dean or an Associate Dean, a job that I was asked to do. I took one academic administrative job. I'm actually memorialized, believe it or not, in the Stanford Record, as having led, and this is according to my expenses, the Nobel Prize winner who was Dean at the time, that I led the biggest and most successful transformation in the history of higher education. I did it. I did it once. I didn't like it. Life is too short. I want to do what I like.
turns.zh: 等等，要是能让时间倒流一周就好了。但时间只会向前流逝。我要掌控自己的时间。对我而言，作为院长或副院长，履行受托职责更为重要。我只担任过一份学术管理职务。说来你可能不信，斯坦福校史记载，在我负责期间，时任院长（且据我的开支记录）的那位诺奖得主，主导了高等教育史上规模最大、最成功的变革。这是我亲手完成的，只此一次。我不喜欢这份工作。人生苦短，我只想做自己喜欢的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really profound point that I think people don't think about, is there's always this drive to acquire power. And your point is that there's a big downside, which is a lack of autonomy. Yeah. You think about the, as I was trying to get Satya Nadella on the podcast, and I talked to his comms people, and they're like, every hour for the next three months is booked already. We know what he's doing. He's extremely booked. And you think about the president, obviously at Elon. I totally get what you're saying.
turns.zh: 这真是一个深刻的观点，我认为人们往往忽视了这一点——人总是有获取权力的欲望。而你指出，这背后隐藏着巨大的代价，那就是失去自主权。是啊。我记得自己曾试图邀请萨蒂亚·纳德拉上播客，和他的公关团队沟通时，他们说未来三个月他的每个小时都已被安排满了。我们都知道他有多忙。而总统职位呢？显然以埃隆·马斯克为例，我完全明白你的意思。

turns.speaker: Jeffrey Pfeffer
turns.en: It is true, and I don't want to do that. And by the way, power also comes with enormous visibility.
